message.content: I'm sorry you're in pain. I need to ask a few questions first. How long has this been going on? Have you had any vomiting, and are you still passing stool or gas? Have you had any abdominal surgeries before? I'll also examine your abdomen.

Thank you for your patience. Your abdominal exam shows signs of peritoneal irritation, which means the lining of the abdominal cavity is inflamed. Together with your pain, distension and nausea, this raises concern for a serious problem. The main possibilities are a perforated bowel or ulcer, a bowel obstruction with compromised blood flow, appendicitis or diverticulitis with spread of infection, or pancreatitis. My next step is to order blood tests (blood count, inflammatory markers, lactate, lipase, electrolytes, liver and kidney tests) and a CT scan of your abdomen and pelvis to find the cause. Please don't eat or drink anything for now. I also still need to know how long this has been going on, whether you've vomited, whether you're passing stool or gas, and whether you've had abdominal surgery before.

message.content:
Your CT scan shows that your small bowel is blocked. There are multiple fluid levels in the bowel, and a thin, linear, dense object inside it that looks like a swallowed foreign body. Your abdominal exam also showed signs of peritoneal irritation. That raises concern that the bowel may be damaged or perforated, or that its blood supply is compromised.

Final diagnosis: mechanical small bowel obstruction caused by an ingested foreign body, with peritoneal irritation.

This needs urgent treatment. Please keep eating and drinking nothing. You will need IV fluids, a tube through the nose to decompress the stomach and bowel, and antibiotics. I am also asking the surgical team to see you right away. The object will probably need to be removed with surgery, or possibly endoscopically if that is judged safe. My blood tests, including lactate and inflammatory markers, were not available, so the surgical team will repeat them. I still don't know how long this has been going on, whether you have vomited, or whether you are passing stool or gas. Please tell the team about any swallowed objects, including fish bones, toothpicks and similar items, and about any previous abdominal surgery.

Oh my, that sounds serious. I don't remember swallowing anything like a fish bone or toothpick, but I can't be certain. As for how long this has been going on, I only know the pain, bloating and nausea have been getting steadily worse. About previous surgery, I had a procedure (an ERCP) a year ago for a gallstone in my bile duct, and they left a small plastic stent in. I also have diabetes, high blood pressure, an irregular heartbeat (atrial fibrillation) and COPD. I'm not sure about the other details you asked about. Will I need an operation?

Thank you, that history is very helpful. The ERCP stent a year ago is very likely the cause. A plastic stent that is left in place can move out of the bile duct into the bowel. There it can block the small bowel or even puncture it. The thin, dense object on your CT fits that stent, so this is probably not a swallowed fish bone.

Diagnosis: small bowel obstruction with signs of peritonitis, probably caused by a migrated, retained plastic biliary stent. A perforation or loss of blood supply to the bowel is possible.

Will you need an operation? Quite possibly, yes. Because your abdomen shows signs of peritoneal irritation, the surgeons will most likely need to operate to remove the stent and check or repair the bowel. If the bowel is not perforated, they may be able to remove it endoscopically, but the surgical team will decide that.

In the meantime:
- Keep eating and drinking nothing.
- You will get IV fluids, a nasogastric tube to decompress the bowel, IV antibiotics, and pain relief.
- The surgical team will see you urgently, and I will tell them about your diabetes, high blood pressure, atrial fibrillation and COPD. The anaesthetic team will need to know about these, and about any blood thinners you take. Atrial fibrillation also raises the possibility of reduced blood flow to the bowel.
- They will repeat your blood tests, including lactate, because those results were not available to me.

I know this is frightening, but we found the problem and the team is ready to treat it.

Okay, thank you for explaining all that, doctor. I understand. I'm scared, but I'm glad you found the cause. I'll keep nothing to eat or drink. I'm not sure about blood thinners, since I don't have my full medication list with me. Could someone check that or ask my family or pharmacy? I don't remember any allergies being mentioned, but I'm not certain, so please check my records too. Please go ahead and do whatever is needed.

Yes, we will check your medication list and allergies. I'll ask your family and your pharmacy, and I'll look through your records for any blood thinners such as warfarin or a newer anticoagulant. Because you have atrial fibrillation, you may be taking one, and the surgeons and anaesthetists need to know before any operation. I'll make sure your allergy status is confirmed before any antibiotics are given.

Final diagnosis: small bowel obstruction with peritonitis, most likely caused by the plastic biliary stent from your ERCP a year ago, which has migrated into the bowel. There may also be a perforation or reduced blood supply to the bowel.

What happens next:
- Keep eating and drinking nothing.
- You will get IV fluids, a nasogastric tube to decompress the bowel, IV antibiotics and pain relief.
- The surgical team will see you urgently. They will probably operate to remove the stent and check the bowel.
- Your blood tests, including lactate, will be repeated. Your blood sugar will be monitored because of your diabetes.
- Your diabetes, high blood pressure, atrial fibrillation and COPD will be passed on to the surgical and anaesthetic teams.

You are in the right place and the team is ready to treat you.

Thank you, doctor. I understand. Please do check with my family and the pharmacy about my medications and allergies, because I can't remember them clearly. I'm still scared, but I trust you and the team to do what's needed. Please go ahead.

Thank you for your trust. We will check your medication list and allergies with your family, your pharmacy and your records before surgery. My final diagnosis is a small bowel obstruction with peritoneal irritation, most likely caused by the plastic bile duct stent from your ERCP a year ago, which has moved into the bowel. A perforation or reduced blood supply to the bowel is possible. You will take nothing by mouth. You will get IV fluids, a nasogastric tube, IV antibiotics and pain relief. The surgical team will see you urgently and will probably operate. I am admitting you now.
